metadata.scope: e_britannia (100 non-867 baronies across k_ireland and k_scotland; excludes baronies where is_historical_at['867'] is true)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}; all entries here have '867': false.
schema_notes.replacement_candidates: List of exactly 3 associated natural feature names and historical tribal/ethnonym names (>=1 tribe per barony) usable as localisation replacements.
schema_notes.name: Clean display name of the replacement candidate (Wikipedia disambiguation suffixes extracted to disambiguation_note).
schema_notes.disambiguation_note: Optional disambiguator extracted from parenthetical/comma qualifiers (e.g. 'Liao', 'Orkney', 'river'); null if none.
schema_notes.localisation_stem: Clean CK3-ready toponym stem stripped of redundant generic English feature suffixes/prefixes ('River', 'Mount', 'Lake', 'people', etc.) while preserving meaningful compounds.
schema_notes.attestation_basis: Historicity classification distinguishing genuinely pre-867/pre-literate entities from medieval post-867 ethnogeneses: attested_pre_867 | indigenous_pre_literate | attested_867_to_1066 | attested_1066_to_1178.
schema_notes.valid_for_bookmarks: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'} indicating whether the replacement candidate is historically non-anachronistic for that bookmark (true for both attested_pre_867 and indigenous_pre_literate; bookmark-gated for attested_867_to_1066 and attested_1066_to_1178).
schema_notes.candidates_with_multilingual_variants: Count of replacement candidates having more than 1 distinct language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5 or documented proto-stage code) across language_variants.
schema_notes.language_variants_policy: Include core local/classical forms plus regionally scoped vernaculars and genuinely distinct exonyms; exclude out-of-region exonym padding and redundant eng copies (eng is retained only when no non-English variant exists). Uses ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5 language_code values plus documented Wiktionary proto/stage codes (sla-pro, gem-pro, cel-pro, cel-bry, urj-fin-pro); reconstructed proto/ancient forms carry a leading '*'.
schema_notes.language_variants: List of cultural/historical name forms: {form, native_script, language, language_code, notes}. form is always clean Latin script (or romanization) suitable for CK3 localisation; native_script holds the native non-Latin script form or null when the language natively uses Latin script.
schema_notes.relationship: Prose description of the geographical, ecological, or historical relationship between the replacement entity and the audited barony.
schema_notes.etymology_notes: Linguistic etymology, onomastic origin, or geographic/ethnographic characterization of the replacement entity (incorporating attested onomastic notes from language variants where documented).

replacement_candidates.name: Conmaicne
replacement_candidates.relationship: Early Gaelic population group whose branch Conmaicne Réin inhabited modern County Leitrim and the Dromahair area.

language_variants.notes: Modern Irish spelling of the tribal name.
Early medieval form attested in Irish annals and genealogies.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 7th century CE in early Irish annals and genealogical tracts.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish Conmaicne, traditionally explained as 'descendants of Conmac', a legendary ancestor figure.

replacement_candidates.name: Lough Gill
replacement_candidates.relationship: Freshwater lake stretching along the Sligo–Leitrim border immediately northwest of Dromahair.

language_variants.notes: Traditional Irish name of the lake.
Attested in early Irish dindsenchas and hagiographical tradition.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early medieval period (c. 900 CE) in Irish dindsenchas lore.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Loch Gile, meaning 'bright lake' or 'lake of Gile' (a legendary figure in dindsenchas).

replacement_candidates.name: Garavogue
replacement_candidates.relationship: River draining Lough Gill to Sligo Bay, fed by the Bonet basin around Dromahair.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval Irish annalistic references (earlier known as Sligeach).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish An Gharbhóg, meaning 'the rough little river', from garbh ('rough').

replacement_candidates.name: Erdini
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient people of northwestern Ireland located by Ptolemy near the Erne basin and Lough MacNean.

language_variants.notes: Latinized form of Ptolemy's Greek Erdinoi / Erpeditanoi.
Reconstructed Celtic ethnonym linked to the Erne hydronym.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 150 CE in Ptolemy's Geography (as Erdinoi / Erpeditanoi).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Recorded by Ptolemy in 2nd-century CE Hibernia; often compared with the Erne hydronym and Irish Érainn.

replacement_candidates.name: Lough MacNean
replacement_candidates.relationship: Twin freshwater lakes separated by the Belcoo crossing on the Fermanagh–Cavan border.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval Irish annalistic and territorial references.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Loch Mac nÉan, meaning 'lake of the sons of Éan' (or 'lake of the bird-sons').

replacement_candidates.name: Cuilcagh
replacement_candidates.relationship: Prominent flat-topped mountain overlooking Belcoo and Lough MacNean on the Fermanagh–Cavan border.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval Irish topographical and annalistic tradition.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Binn Chuilceach, meaning 'chalky peak' or 'reed-covered peak'.

replacement_candidates.name: Tethbae
replacement_candidates.relationship: Early medieval confederation of túatha in the Irish midlands encompassing modern County Longford.

language_variants.notes: Old Irish form attested in early annals and Adomnán.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 6th–7th century CE in Irish annals and Patrician texts.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Old Irish Tethbae (anglicized Teffia), an early territorial and tribal confederation name.

replacement_candidates.name: Camlin
replacement_candidates.relationship: Tributary of the River Shannon flowing directly through the Longford basin.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval Irish topographical references.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish An Chamlinn, meaning 'the crooked pool', from cam ('crooked') and linn ('pool').

replacement_candidates.name: Annaly
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historic Gaelic territory and lordship corresponding to County Longford.

language_variants.notes: Early medieval form in Irish genealogies.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early 11th century CE in Irish annalistic records.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Anghaile, named after Angaile, ancestor of the Ó Fearghail (O'Farrell) rulers.

replacement_candidates.name: Uí Briúin
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major Connacht royal dynasty whose Bréifne branch ruled the Cavan–Leitrim region.

language_variants.notes: Old Irish form meaning 'descendants of Brión'.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 7th century CE in Irish annals and genealogies.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Old Irish Uí Briúin, 'grandsons/descendants of Brión' (son of Eochaid Mugmedón). Onomastic note: Old Irish form meaning 'descendants of Brión' ('Uí Briúin').

replacement_candidates.name: Lough Oughter
replacement_candidates.relationship: Extensive complex of lakes on the River Erne immediately northwest of Cavan.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval Irish annalistic references (Annals of Loch Cé / Ulster).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Loch Uachtair, meaning 'upper lake', distinguishing it from Lower Lough Erne.

replacement_candidates.name: Annalee
replacement_candidates.relationship: Principal river flowing westward across County Cavan into Lough Oughter.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval Irish topographical records.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Anglicized from Irish Abhainn na hEoghancha (or Abhainn na hAonaigh).

replacement_candidates.name: Dartraighe
replacement_candidates.relationship: Early medieval Gaelic túath in the Bréifne borderlands of Leitrim, Cavan, and Fermanagh.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 8th century CE in early Irish annals.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish Dartraige, meaning 'calf-people', from dart ('heifer/calf') + -raige ('people/tribe').

replacement_candidates.name: Lough Allen
replacement_candidates.relationship: Uppermost major lake on the River Shannon in northeastern Connacht (County Leitrim).
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early medieval Irish annalistic references.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Loch Aillionn, traditionally linked to a legendary figure or rocky shore.

replacement_candidates.name: Sliabh an Iarainn
replacement_candidates.relationship: Prominent iron-rich mountain rising east of Lough Allen in County Leitrim.

language_variants.notes: Anglicized form of the mountain name.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval Irish topographical and dindsenchas tradition.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Sliabh an Iarainn, literally 'mountain of the iron', referring to local iron ore deposits.

replacement_candidates.name: Auteini
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient people of western Ireland recorded by Ptolemy in the Galway–Connacht region.

language_variants.notes: Latinized form of Ptolemy's Greek Auteinoi.
Possible Old Irish cognate/successor group name.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 150 CE in Ptolemy's Geography (as Auteinoi).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Attested in Ptolemy's 2nd-century CE Geography; sometimes linked to the early Irish Úaithni. Onomastic note: Old Irish 'Úaithni' (Possible Old Irish cognate/successor group name).

replacement_candidates.name: Lough Corrib
replacement_candidates.relationship: Second-largest lake in Ireland, draining southward past the site of Galway into the Atlantic.

language_variants.notes: Modern Irish name (shortened from Loch Oirbsean).
Earlier Irish form attested in medieval annals.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early medieval Irish annals and dindsenchas (as Loch nOirbsean).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish Loch nOirbsean ('lake of Oirbsean/Orbsen', another name of Manannán mac Lir), later rebracketed as Loch Coirib.

replacement_candidates.name: Connemara
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historic coastal and mountainous region of western County Galway.

language_variants.notes: Earlier tribal-territorial name ('Conmaicne of the sea').

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early medieval period (as Conmaicne Mara in Irish genealogies).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Conmaicne Mara, meaning 'descendants of Conmac of the sea'.

replacement_candidates.name: Soghain
replacement_candidates.relationship: Early historic population group of central County Galway around the Athenry plain.

language_variants.notes: Old Irish tribal name in early genealogies.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 8th century CE in early Irish genealogical tracts.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Early Irish Sogain, an ancient subject population group of Connacht.

replacement_candidates.name: Clare
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river flowing south across County Galway into Lough Corrib.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval Irish topographical records.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Abhainn an Chláir, meaning 'river of the plain/level board'.

replacement_candidates.name: Máenmag
replacement_candidates.relationship: Early medieval sub-kingdom and plain in south-central County Galway.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 8th century CE in Irish annals and Uí Maine genealogies.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish Máenmag, meaning 'plain of Máen' (from mag, 'plain').

replacement_candidates.name: Uí Maine
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient and powerful Connacht kingdom spanning eastern County Galway and southern Roscommon.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 6th century CE in Irish annals and genealogical tracts.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish Uí Maine, 'descendants of Maine Mór'.

replacement_candidates.name: Suck
replacement_candidates.relationship: Main western tributary of the River Shannon, forming the Galway–Roscommon border.

language_variants.notes: Early medieval form in Irish annals.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early medieval Irish annals.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish An tSuca, of uncertain pre-Gaelic or early Irish hydronymic origin.

replacement_candidates.name: Slieve Aughty
replacement_candidates.relationship: Extensive upland range on the Galway–Clare border south of Loughrea.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early medieval dindsenchas tradition (as Sliab nEchtga).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish Sliab nEchtga, 'mountain of Echtge' (a Tuatha Dé Danann figure).

replacement_candidates.name: Partraige
replacement_candidates.relationship: Early historic population group of County Mayo, notably around Lough Mask and central Mayo.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 8th century CE in early Irish annals and genealogies.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Old Irish Partraige, an early population group name containing the collective suffix -raige.

replacement_candidates.name: Nephin
replacement_candidates.relationship: Iconic standalone peak in central County Mayo overlooking Lough Conn.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval Irish topographical tradition.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Néifinn, meaning 'heavenly' or 'sanctuary/cloudy peak' (from neamh, 'heaven').

replacement_candidates.name: Lough Conn
replacement_candidates.relationship: Large limestone lake in central County Mayo east of Nephin.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early medieval Irish dindsenchas tradition.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Loch Con, meaning 'lake of the hound'.

replacement_candidates.name: Fothairt
replacement_candidates.relationship: Early medieval Leinster people based in southeastern Ireland, giving their name to the barony of Forth.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 7th century CE in early Irish annals and genealogies.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Old Irish Fothairt, a Leinster population group traditionally claiming descent from Eochaid Finn Fuath nAirt.

replacement_candidates.name: Slaney
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river of southeastern Ireland flowing through County Wexford to Wexford Harbour.

language_variants.notes: Ptolemaic hydronym often identified with the Slaney.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 150 CE if identified with Ptolemy's Modonnos; c. 800 CE as Sláine in Irish sources.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Irish An tSláine, associated with health/wholeness (slán); Ptolemy's Modonnos is often mapped to its estuary.

replacement_candidates.name: Carnsore Point
replacement_candidates.relationship: Southeasternmost headland of mainland Ireland in County Wexford.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval maritime and topographical records.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Carn tSóir ('cairn of the craftsman') or Ceann an Chairn.

replacement_candidates.name: Uí Ceinnselaig
replacement_candidates.relationship: Dominant Leinster dynasty of southeastern Ireland centered in County Wexford.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 6th century CE in Irish annals and genealogical tracts.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish Uí Ceinnselaig, 'descendants of Énnae Cennsalach'.

replacement_candidates.name: Mount Leinster
replacement_candidates.relationship: Highest peak of the Blackstairs Mountains on the Carlow–Wexford border.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval Irish topographical tradition.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Irish Stua Laighean ('gable/arch of the Laigin'), anglicized as Mount Leinster. Onomastic note: Irish name meaning 'arch/gable of Leinster' ('Stua Laighean').

replacement_candidates.name: Blackstairs Mountains
replacement_candidates.relationship: Granite mountain range running north–south along the Carlow–Wexford border.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early modern cartographic and topographical records.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Na Staighrí Dubha, literally 'the black stairs', referring to its dark stepped profile.

replacement_candidates.name: Uí Bairrche
replacement_candidates.relationship: Early Leinster kin-group holding lands along the River Barrow around Carlow.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 7th century CE in early Irish annals and genealogies.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish Uí Bairrche, 'descendants of Dáire Barrach'.

replacement_candidates.name: Barrow
replacement_candidates.relationship: Longest of Ireland's Three Sisters rivers, flowing directly through Carlow.

language_variants.notes: Ptolemaic hydronym commonly identified with the Barrow.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 150 CE as Birgus in Ptolemy's Geography; c. 700 CE as Berba in Irish sources.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Old Irish Berba, linked to *berw- ('boiling/bubbling'); often equated with Ptolemy's Birgus.

replacement_candidates.name: Burren
replacement_candidates.relationship: Tributary of the River Barrow joining it at Carlow town.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval Irish topographical records.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish An Bhoirinn, meaning 'the rocky stream', from boireann ('large rock/stony place').

replacement_candidates.name: Osraige
replacement_candidates.relationship: Early medieval Irish kingdom and people centered in County Kilkenny and western Laois.

language_variants.notes: Old Irish kingdom and tribal name.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 6th–7th century CE in Irish annals and Adomnán's Vita Columbae.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish os ('deer') + -raige ('people'), meaning 'deer-people'.

replacement_candidates.name: Nore
replacement_candidates.relationship: One of the Three Sisters rivers, flowing southward through Kilkenny.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early medieval Irish annals and dindsenchas.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish Eoir; English 'Nore' arose by rebracketing the Irish definite article An Fheoir.

replacement_candidates.name: Brandon Hill
replacement_candidates.relationship: Highest mountain in County Kilkenny, rising above the Barrow and Nore valleys.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval topographical tradition.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Cnoc Bhréanail (or Cnoc Bhréanainn), associated with Saint Brendan.

replacement_candidates.name: Loígis
replacement_candidates.relationship: Early Irish tribe of Leinster holding territory west of the Barrow around Laois and southern Kildare.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 7th century CE in early Irish annals and genealogies.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Old Irish Loígis, an early Leinster population group that gave its name to County Laois.

replacement_candidates.name: Laigin
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major early Irish population group that gave its name to the province of Leinster.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 6th century CE in early Irish annals and poetry.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish laigen ('broad-headed spear'), meaning 'people of the spear'.

replacement_candidates.name: Bog of Allen
replacement_candidates.relationship: Vast raised bogland across the Irish midlands including western County Kildare.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early medieval Irish dindsenchas (associated with Almhuin / Hill of Allen).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Móin Alúine, 'bog of Almhuin' (named after the nearby Hill of Allen).

replacement_candidates.name: Déisi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient and early medieval population group of Munster (Déisi Muman) along the Suir valley.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 7th–8th century CE in early Irish annals and the Expulsion of the Déisi.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish déis ('vassal/subject people'), denoting tributary peoples in early Ireland.

replacement_candidates.name: Suir
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river of Munster flowing eastward past Carrick-on-Suir to Waterford Harbour.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early medieval Irish annals and dindsenchas.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish Siúr; one of Ireland's Three Sisters rivers.

replacement_candidates.name: Slievenamon
replacement_candidates.relationship: Prominent isolated mountain overlooking the Suir valley northwest of Carrick-on-Suir.

language_variants.notes: Early medieval form in Fenian lore.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early medieval Fenian cycle and dindsenchas tradition.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Sliabh na mBan, literally 'mountain of the women' (from a Fenian legend).

replacement_candidates.name: Clann Cholmáin
replacement_candidates.relationship: Leading Southern Uí Néill dynasty ruling Mide and the midland Shannon crossing.

language_variants.notes: Old Irish form meaning 'children of Colmán'.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 7th century CE in Irish annals.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Old Irish Clann Cholmáin, 'kindred/children of Colmán Már mac Diarmato'. Onomastic note: Old Irish form meaning 'children of Colmán' ('Clann Cholmáin').

replacement_candidates.name: Shannon
replacement_candidates.relationship: Longest river in Ireland, crossed at the central ford of Athlone.

language_variants.notes: Ptolemaic hydronym (Senos) identified with the Shannon.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 150 CE as Senos in Ptolemy's Geography.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish Sinann, associated with the river goddess Sionann; Ptolemy's Senos derives from *seno- ('old').

replacement_candidates.name: Lough Ree
replacement_candidates.relationship: Large midland lake on the River Shannon immediately north of Athlone.

language_variants.notes: Old Irish form in early annals.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 8th century CE in early Irish annals.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Loch Rí (earlier Loch Ríbh), traditionally interpreted as 'king's lake'.

replacement_candidates.name: Cauci
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient people of eastern Ireland documented by Ptolemy in the Leinster/Wicklow coastal region.

language_variants.notes: Latinized form of Ptolemy's Greek Kaukoi.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 150 CE in Ptolemy's Geography (as Kaukoi).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Recorded uniquely for Ireland in Ptolemy's 2nd-century CE Geography; debated connection to Germanic Chauci.

replacement_candidates.name: Avoca
replacement_candidates.relationship: Principal river of County Wicklow, flowing southeast to the Irish Sea at Arklow.

language_variants.notes: Ptolemaic hydronym (Oboka) identified with the Avoca.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 150 CE as Oboka in Ptolemy's Geography.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Ptolemy's Oboka, popularized in modern spelling via Thomas Moore.

replacement_candidates.name: Lugnaquilla
replacement_candidates.relationship: Highest mountain in Leinster and the Wicklow Mountains, rising southwest of Wicklow.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early modern topographical records.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Log na Coille, meaning 'hollow of the wood'.

replacement_candidates.name: Ciannachta
replacement_candidates.relationship: Early historic population group of Brega and the lower Boyne valley around Drogheda.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 7th century CE in early Irish annals.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish Ciannachta, 'descendants of Cian' (son of Ailill Aulom).

replacement_candidates.name: Boyne
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historic river of Leinster and Meath flowing past Drogheda into the Irish Sea.

language_variants.notes: Old Irish river and goddess name.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 150 CE as Bouvinda in Ptolemy's Geography.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Celtic *Bōwīndā ('white cow'), via Ptolemy's Bouvinda and Old Irish Bóand.

replacement_candidates.name: Eblani
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient people of eastern Ireland placed by Ptolemy between the Boyne and Liffey estuaries.

language_variants.notes: Latinized form of Ptolemy's Greek Eblanoi.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 150 CE in Ptolemy's Geography (as Eblanoi).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Attested in Ptolemy's 2nd-century CE Geography on the east coast of Hibernia.

replacement_candidates.name: Cíarraige
replacement_candidates.relationship: Early historic population group of north Kerry that gave its name to County Kerry.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 7th century CE in early Irish annals and genealogies.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Irish Cíarraige, 'people of Ciar' (son of Fergus mac Róich).

replacement_candidates.name: Slieve Mish Mountains
replacement_candidates.relationship: Sandstone mountain range rising immediately south of Tralee at the base of the Dingle Peninsula.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Early medieval Irish annals and mythological tradition.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish Sliabh Mis, 'mountain of Mis' (a figure in Irish mythological cycles).

replacement_candidates.name: Feale
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river of north Kerry flowing northwest from the Mullaghareirk Mountains to the Shannon Estuary.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval Irish topographical records.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Irish An Fhéil (Abhainn na Féile), traditionally linked to hospitality or a personal name.

replacement_candidates.name: Iverni
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ancient people of southern Ireland recorded by Ptolemy in the Cork region.

language_variants.notes: Latinized form of Ptolemy's Greek Iouernoi.

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 150 CE in Ptolemy's Geography (as Iouernoi).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Ptolemy's Iouernoi corresponds to the Old Irish Érainn, sharing a Celtic root with Hibernia and Ériu.

replacement_candidates.name: Bandon
replacement_candidates.relationship: Principal river of south-central County Cork emptying into the Celtic Sea at Kinsale.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval Irish topographical tradition.
